title_en: Taishan Gypsum Co., Ltd. v. Shandong Wanjia Building Materials Co., Ltd. and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce — administrative dispute over trademark
ruling_gist_en: Article 10, paragraph 1, subparagraph (8) of the Trademark Law provides that a mark that is detrimental to socialist morals and customs or has other adverse effects shall not be used as a trademark. When determining whether a relevant mark constitutes a circumstance of having other adverse effects, consideration shall be given to whether the mark or its constituent elements may have a negative or adverse impact on China's political, economic, cultural, religious, ethnic and other social public interests and public order. If a mark has religious connotations, then regardless of whether the relevant public can generally perceive it, or whether the mark has been used and gained a certain degree of popularity, it can generally be considered that the registration of such a mark is harmful to religious feelings, religious beliefs, or folk beliefs, and thus has adverse effects.

full_text_en:
Tai Shan Gypsum Co., Ltd. v. Shandong Wanjia Building Materials Co., Ltd. and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce — Dispute over Administrative Trademark Dispute

【Ruling Summary】

Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law provides that a mark that is detrimental to socialist morals or has other adverse effects shall not be used as a trademark. In determining whether a mark constitutes a circumstance of having other adverse effects, consideration shall be given to whether the mark or its constituent elements may have a negative or adverse impact on the social public interest and public order of China's politics, economy, culture, religion, ethnicity, etc. If a mark has religious connotations, regardless of whether the relevant public can generally perceive it, or whether the mark has been used and has acquired a certain reputation, it can generally be considered that the registration of such mark is detrimental to religious feelings, religious beliefs, or folk beliefs, and thus has adverse effects.

Administrative Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2016) Zui Gao Fa Xing Zai No. 21

Re-Applicant (Third Party at First Instance): Tai Shan Gypsum Co., Ltd. Address: Dawenkou, Daiyue District, Tai'an City, Shandong Province.

Legal Representative: Jia Tongchun, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Wang Hua, Attorney at Beijing Hengdu (Tianjin) Law Firm.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Shandong Wanjia Building Materials Co., Ltd. Address: Wanzhuang Village, Baotai Town, Pingyi County, Linyi City, Shandong Province.

Legal Representative: Guan Guolei, Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Yang Kai, Attorney at Beijing Liu Shen Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zheng Peng, Intern Attorney at Beijing Liu Shen Law Firm.

Defendant at First Instance, Respondent at Second Instance: The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce. Address: No. 1 Chama Nanjie, Xicheng District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: He Xunban, Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Nana, Examiner of the Board.

The Re-Applicant, Tai Shan Gypsum Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tai Shan Gypsum), filed a re-application for retrial with this Court against the administrative judgment (2014) Gao Xing (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 3390 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court in a dispute with the Respondent, Shandong Wanjia Building Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Wanjia Company), and the Defendant at First Instance, Respondent at Second Instance, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the TRAB). Upon review, this Court decided on December 8, 2015, by administrative ruling (2015) Zhi Xing Zi No. 62, to grant retrial of the case. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law to hear the case, and the trial has now concluded.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts upon trial: The trademark "Taishan Dadi" (No. 3011175) (i.e., the disputed trademark) was applied for registration on November 5, 2001, by Tai'an Taishan Yuanshuai Gypsum Board Factory, and was approved for registration on March 21, 2003, for use on gypsum board products in Class 19. On July 2, 2008, the trademark was approved for transfer to Shandong North New Building Materials Co., Ltd. On April 14, 2010, the trademark was approved for transfer to Wanjia Company.

On May 17, 2013, Tai Shan Gypsum filed a dispute application with the TRAB, mainly arguing that the disputed trademark is detrimental to religious beliefs, religious feelings, or folk beliefs, and is likely to cause the public to misunderstand the characteristics of the goods or the qualifications of the provider. Additionally, it argued that Wanjia Company acted with strong subjective bad faith, and its conduct seriously disrupts the normal trademark management order and market economic order of China, and harms the legitimate interests of the relevant public. According to Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law (as amended in 2001), the disputed trademark should be invalidated.

Tai Shan Gypsum submitted the following main evidence to the TRAB: a statement issued by the Tai'an City Ethnic and Religious Affairs Bureau, online reports about "Taishan Dadi," trademarks applied for maliciously by Wanjia Company, an enterprise state-owned property trading transaction certificate, evidence of the well-known trademark "Taishan and Device," etc.

Wanjia Company argued in response that the disputed trademark is used lawfully and does not constitute harm to religious beliefs, religious feelings, or folk beliefs. It requested the TRAB to maintain the registration of the disputed trademark.

Wanjia Company submitted the following main evidence to the TRAB: online searches of "Taishan Dadi" and "Dongyue Dadi," materials on the invalidation of "Taishan Dadi," honor certificates of Wanjia Company, the dispute ruling, evidence of trademark use, etc.

On April 14, 2014, the TRAB issued Ruling No. 051795, "Ruling on the Dispute over Trademark No. 3011175 'Taishan Dadi'" (hereinafter referred to as Ruling No. 051795).

The ruling found that the evidence submitted by Tai Shan Gypsum proved that "Taishan Dadi" is also known as "Dongyue Taishan Dadi" or "God of Mount Tai," with the full name "Dongyue Taishan Tianqi Rensheng Dadi." It is one of the deities in Taoism, a unique divine name in the Mount Tai region of Shandong. Its use as a trademark could easily hurt the feelings of religious people, thus causing adverse effects. Moreover, Wanjia Company is also located in Shandong and should have been aware of the religious significance of "Taishan Dadi" and the adverse social impact its registration as a trademark would cause. Therefore, the disputed trademark falls under the circumstance stipulated in Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law. Accordingly, the TRAB ruled to invalidate the registration of the disputed trademark pursuant to Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) and Article 43 of the Trademark Law.

Dissatisfied with Ruling No. 051795, Wanjia Company filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, alleging that the disputed trademark is used lawfully and does not constitute harm to religious beliefs, religious feelings, or folk beliefs. The TRAB, based solely on the certificate issued by the Tai'an City Ethnic and Religious Affairs Bureau, determined that using "Taishan Dadi" as a trademark could easily hurt the feelings of religious people and cause adverse social impact. This determination clearly does not conform to objective facts or legal provisions. The disputed trademark has been registered and used for more than ten years without harming religious feelings or causing adverse social impact. On the contrary, it has achieved good social benefits and positive public evaluation. Wanjia Company requested the court to annul Ruling No. 051795.

During the first-instance proceedings, Wanjia Company submitted books and materials on Taoism and trademark registration information for "Taishan Dadi," which had not been submitted during the trademark dispute proceedings. Tai Shan Gypsum submitted articles and theses from CNKI, trademark transfer announcements, and business registration records of Wanjia Company and Shandong North New Building Materials Co., Ltd., which had not been submitted during the trademark dispute proceedings.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held:

I. Application of Law in this Case

The Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, as amended on August 30, 2013, came into effect on May 1, 2014. Given that Ruling No. 051795 in this case was issued during the period when the 2001 Trademark Law was in effect, pursuant to Article 84 of the Legislation Law of the People's Republic of China (in effect in 2000), this case shall be tried under the 2001 Trademark Law.

II. Whether the Disputed Trademark Violates Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law

Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law stipulates that a mark that is detrimental to socialist morals or has other adverse effects shall not be used as a trademark. This provision pertains to marks that have a negative or adverse impact on the public interest or public order of China. Whether a disputed trademark can be registered should be determined by considering factors such as China's historical and cultural traditions and social background.

In this case, the evidence on record shows that the Five Mountain Emperors refer to the Great Emperor of Dongyue Taishan, the Great Emperor of Nanyue Hengshan, the Great Emperor of Xiyue Huashan, the Great Emperor of Beiyue Hengshan, and the Great Emperor of Zhongyue Songshan. This belief originated from the worship of mountains and rivers in ancient China, reflecting people's fear and awe of towering, majestic, and mysterious peaks. Among them, the "Great Emperor of Dongyue Taishan," also known as "Taishan Dadi," is one of the deities in Taoism. It has been not only enshrined or conferred by successive emperors but also long revered and worshipped by the common people and Taoist believers, holding a very high religious status. Wanjia Company and the original applicant for the disputed trademark are both located in Shandong and should have been aware of the religious significance of "Taishan Dadi." Applying for and using "Taishan Dadi" as a trademark could easily hurt the religious feelings of religious people and Taoist believers, thereby causing adverse effects. Therefore, the disputed trademark falls under the circumstance provided in Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law. The TRAB's ruling to invalidate the disputed trademark was correct and should be upheld. Regarding Wanjia Company's argument that the disputed trademark has been registered for many years and has not caused adverse effects through long-term promotion and use, the first-instance court held that Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law is an absolute prohibition clause. It does not provide an exception for a mark with adverse effects to be registered through use. Therefore, Wanjia Company's argument lacks legal basis.

Pursuant to Article 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (prior to amendment), the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered a judgment upholding Ruling No. 051795. The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 was borne by Wanjia Company (already paid).

Dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, Wanjia Company appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, requesting the revocation of the first-instance judgment and Ruling No. 051795, and an order for the TRAB to issue a new ruling. Its main reasons were: (1) The disputed trademark is not a religious term. The deity in Taoism is "Dongyue Dadi" or "God of Mount Tai," and there is no evidence proving that "Taishan Dadi" is "Dongyue Dadi." The TRAB and the first-instance court erred in this finding. (2) The use of the disputed trademark has not caused adverse effects. The disputed trademark has been registered and used for more than ten years without harming religious feelings or causing adverse social impact. On the contrary, through use, the disputed trademark has established a high market reputation and achieved good social benefits and positive public evaluation. (3) Tai Shan Gypsum had previously filed a dispute application based on the disputed trademark being similar to the "Tai Shan and Device" trademark, which was not supported by the TRAB. Tai Shan Gypsum's subsequent use of the public interest clause of the Trademark Law to seek private gain, targeting a market competitor, was clearly malicious.

The TRAB and Tai Shan Gypsum complied with the first-instance judgment.

The facts found by the Beijing High People's Court upon second-instance trial were essentially the same as those found by the first-instance court.

During the second-instance proceedings, Wanjia Company submitted excerpts from publications and books, including the "Annals of Tai'an City," "Annals of Tai'an Region," "Dictionary of Chinese Deities," "Mount Tai Belief and Chinese Society," "Study on Dai Temple of Mount Tai," and "Taoist Culture," to demonstrate that in official records of Tai'an City and religious-related books, the appellation "Taishan Dadi" for a religious deity does not appear, and that the registration and use of the disputed trademark have not caused adverse effects. Tai Shan Gypsum acknowledged the authenticity of the above evidence but argued it lacked relevance to the case.

Additionally, it was found that on December 8, 2008, Tai Shan Gypsum had filed an application for invalidation with the TRAB on the grounds that the registration of the disputed trademark violated Article 13, Paragraph 2 and Article 28 of the Trademark Law. The TRAB issued Dispute Ruling No. 10872 (2010), ruling to invalidate the disputed trademark. Wanjia Company, dissatisfied, filed an administrative lawsuit. During the lawsuit, the TRAB submitted a statement of error in its ruling to the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. Wanjia Company withdrew its lawsuit, which was permitted by the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. On September 5, 2011, the TRAB issued Dispute Ruling No. 20788 (2011), ruling to maintain the registration of the disputed trademark on the grounds that Tai Shan Gypsum's invalidation application exceeded the five-year time limit and lacked basis for the relevant grounds. This ruling became final.

The Beijing High People's Court held:

This case is tried under the Trademark Law as amended in 2001. Based on the claims and defenses of the parties, the focus of this case is whether the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes the "adverse effects" circumstance under Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law.

Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law provides that a mark that is detrimental to socialist morals or has other adverse effects shall not be used as a trademark. "Having other adverse effects" refers to marks whose words, graphics, or other constituent elements have a negative or adverse impact on the social public interest and public order of China, including politics, economy, culture, religion, and ethnicity.

Marks that are detrimental to religious beliefs, religious feelings, or folk beliefs generally shall not be used as trademarks. In determining whether such marks are harmful, consideration shall be given to whether the mark is genuinely and definitively used or directly associated by believers or worshippers in the religious field, and whether it objectively affects the social public interest, such as religious beliefs, religious feelings, or folk beliefs. According to the facts found, in the local religious beliefs of Shandong Province, there indeed exists the appellation "Dongyue Dadi" or "God of Mount Tai," but there is no official state record definitively establishing "Taishan Dadi" as a deity appellation. The statements and online reports submitted by Tai Shan Gypsum lack historical verification, and the said reports are mainly literary fabrications, unsupported by other evidence. Concurrently, Wanjia Company submitted religious books such as the "Annals of Tai'an City" and "Annals of Tai'an Region," whose authenticity was acknowledged by Tai Shan Gypsum. In the records and introductions of "Dongyue Dadi" or "God of Mount Tai," "Taishan Dadi" is never mentioned, which at least proves that "Taishan Dadi" does not have a unique or objective correspondence with the said deity appellations. Considering the evidence as a whole, it is insufficient to prove that "Taishan Dadi" is genuinely and definitively used or directly associated by believers or worshippers in the religious field. The first-instance court and the TRAB lacked basis for finding that "Taishan Dadi" is a unique deity name in the Mount Tai region of Shandong Taoism, and this finding should be corrected.

Tai Shan Gypsum had previously filed an invalidation application on December 8, 2008, on the grounds that the registration of the disputed trademark violated Article 13, Paragraph 2 and Article 28 of the Trademark Law. The TRAB issued a ruling maintaining the registration of the disputed trademark. That application and the final ruling did not mention the "adverse effects" ground under the Trademark Law. Under these circumstances, Tai Shan Gypsum's subsequent application for dispute based on the "adverse effects" ground, purportedly to protect the public interest but actually aimed at protecting its specific civil rights, should be examined. The evidence submitted by Wanjia Company can prove that the disputed trademark has acquired high visibility through use, achieving good social benefits and positive evaluation. To maintain the established and stable market order, and in conjunction with the above finding on the mark itself, it should be held that the registration of the disputed trademark does not violate Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law. The first-instance court and the TRAB erred in this finding, and this should be corrected. Wanjia Company's relevant appeal arguments are tenable and should be upheld.

Pursuant to Article 61(3) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (prior to amendment) and Article 70 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Beijing High People's Court rendered a judgment setting aside the first-instance judgment and Ruling No. 051795, and ordered the TRAB to issue a new ruling on the dispute.

Taishan Gypsum Company stated in its application for retrial: (1) The registration of the disputed trademark violates Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law. The judgment of the second instance was erroneous in both the factual findings and the application of law and should be reversed. 1. The judgment of the second instance did not form a corresponding understanding and application of the law regarding "signs that are detrimental to religious belief, religious sentiment, or folk belief." On one hand, the judgment of the second instance held that the public group for determining whether a sign constitutes "detrimental to religious belief, religious sentiment, or folk belief" is "believers or worshipers in the religious field," and the form of manifestation is "use" or a "direct connection." On the other hand, the judgment of the second instance held that "Taishan Dadi" had not been "officially recorded by the state," and further held that the "Tai'an City Annals" and "Tai'an Prefecture Annals" did not mention "Taishan Dadi," thereby denying the fact that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a deity. The groups involved in these findings are not "believers or worshipers in the religious field." Regarding the argument on "use," the evidence submitted by the company had proven that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a deity, but the court of second instance considered it lacked historical verification and therefore did not adopt it. However, according to the aforementioned understanding, the standard for determining whether a "use act" is established is whether the "use act" objectively exists, without requiring "historical verification." 2. Whether "Taishan Dadi" is the "unique appellation" of a deity is not a prerequisite for determining "adverse effects"; the existence of such an appellation cannot be denied solely because it is not the only corresponding name. Moreover, regarding "other adverse effects," the relevant legal provisions also do not require that a sign and a religious symbol must have a one-to-one correspondence. 3. "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. First, from the literal meaning of the appellation, "Dongyue" and "Taishan" have a one-to-one correspondence. Using Baidu to search for "Dongyue Dadi" as a keyword yields numerous results including "Taishan Dadi." Second, from the perspective of official institutions in the Taishan region, "Taishan Dadi" is a commonly used appellation for Taoist deities. Both the Tai'an City Ethnic and Religious Affairs Bureau and the Tai'an City Taishan Scenic Area Management Committee have issued letters confirming that "Taishan Dadi" is a religious idol belief and an object of worship. Third, from the perspective of sociologists, relevant experts, and the general public, "Taishan Dadi" is recognized as an appellation for a Taoist deity. Newspapers such as the "People's Daily" have recorded that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity, used interchangeably with "Taishan Shen," "Dongyue Dadi," and "Tianqi Rensheng Dadi." In addition to Shandong Province, places such as Jiangsu, Fujian, Shanxi, Zhejiang, Beijing, Guangdong, Shaanxi, and Liaoning also use "Taishan Dadi" to refer to one of the unique Taoist deities of Mount Tai in Shandong. Fourth, Wanjia Company also acknowledged that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. In the defense statement for the opposition against the registration of Trademark No. 9044267 "Taishan Dadi," Wanjia Company recognized that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. Fifth, the term "Dadi" originated from Taoism, and the word itself is associated with Taoism. (2) The court of second instance misinterpreted the intention behind its challenge and the application of the law. 1. The judgment of the second instance held that its "intention was to protect its specific civil rights and interests by safeguarding social public interests" and used this as a reason to find that the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate the "adverse effects" provision, which constitutes an error in the application of law. 2. From the perspective of the registration origin of the disputed trademark, its registration resulted in multiple legal consequences, including harming the normal registration order and the rights and interests of Taishan Gypsum Company, and was clearly an improper registration act. In addition to the disputed trademark in this case, Wanjia Company also applied for a series of trademarks highly similar to the well-known "Taishan" and "Beixin" trademarks in the gypsum board industry, such as "Taishan Beixin," "Taishan Di," "Dongyue Taishan," "Taishan Jiamei," "Wuyuezhizun Taishan," and "Beixinzhixing Taishan." It also applied for trademarks identical to well-known scenic spots such as "Putuo Shan," "Huangpu Jiang," "Waitan," and "Huaguo Shan." Wanjia Company's numerous applications were clearly not based on the operational needs of the enterprise. 3. In the administrative dispute case regarding the opposition against Trademark No. 9044267 "Taishan Dadi," it had already been determined that "Taishan Dadi" and Taishan Gypsum Company's "Taishan" trademark constituted similar trademarks on similar goods. The disputed trademark in this case is identical in designation to Trademark No. 9044267 and also constitutes an infringement of its rights. Considering the substantive rights and interests, the registration should also be revoked. (3) During the review, first instance, and second instance proceedings of this case, Wanjia Company failed to provide corresponding evidence to prove its use of the trademark. The judgment of the second instance, which found that "the disputed trademark has gained relatively high recognition through use," constitutes an error in fact-finding. Furthermore, Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law, as an absolute prohibition on registration, does not and should not need to consider the actual use of the trademark when applied. Taishan Gypsum Company requests that this court lawfully reverse the second-instance judgment, uphold Ruling No. 051795 and the first-instance judgment, and order Wanjia Company to bear the litigation costs of this case.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board submitted opinions, stating: The evidence submitted by Taishan Gypsum Company proves that "Taishan Dadi" is also known as "Dongyue Taishan Dadi" or "Taishan Shen," with the full appellation "Dongyue Taishan Tianqi Rensheng Dadi." It is one of the Taoist deities and a unique deity name of the Shandong Mount Tai region. Using it as a trademark is likely to hurt the religious feelings of religious persons, thereby causing adverse effects. Moreover, Wanjia Company is also located in Shandong Province and should be aware of the religious significance of "Taishan Dadi" and the adverse social impact that its registration as a trademark may cause. Therefore, the disputed trademark falls within the circumstances stipulated in Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law. Ruling No. 051795 is sufficiently grounded, with clear findings of fact, correct application of law, and conforms to legal procedures. The Board requests this court to lawfully reverse the second-instance judgment, uphold Ruling No. 051795 and the first-instance judgment, and order Wanjia Company to bear the litigation costs of this case.

Wanjia Company submitted opinions, stating: (1) "Taishan Dadi" is not an appellation for a Taoist deity, and the findings of fact in the second-instance judgment were clear. 1. In Taoism, there is indeed a deity unique to the Mount Tai region, but the official appellation for this deity, historically and currently, is "Dongyue Dadi" or "Taishan Shen," or its full title "Dongyue Taishan Tianqi Rensheng Dadi." The books and local chronicles it submitted in the second instance, including the "Tai'an City Annals," "Tai'an Prefecture Annals," "Dictionary of Chinese Deities and Monsters," "Taishan Belief and Chinese Society," "Study of the Dai Temple at Mount Tai," and "Taoist Culture," all refer to the deity of Mount Tai as "Dongyue Dadi" or "Taishan Shen," with no instance using "Taishan Dadi." These publications are all formal publications with high credibility. Furthermore, on the official websites of the China Taoist Association and various local Taoist associations (including those in Beijing and Shandong regions), the appellation used is "Dongyue Dadi," not "Taishan Dadi." The most fundamental criterion for determining whether a term is a religious term is the recognition of religious figures and believers. Since neither the local Taoist associations nor the Dongyue Temples use "Taishan Dadi," it is evident that "Taishan Dadi" itself is not a religious term. "Taishan Dadi" is a term coined by Wanjia Company and does not have an exclusive relationship with "Dongyue Dadi" in Taoism. 2. The evidence submitted by Taishan Gypsum Company is insufficient to prove that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. Taishan Gypsum Company's argument that "Taishan" and "Dongyue" have exclusivity, thus equating "Taishan Dadi" with "Dongyue Dadi," lacks sufficient basis. The appellation of deities in religion is extremely sacred. "Dongyue Dadi" has been the deity worshipped by Taoist believers for thousands of years, and this appellation has become fixed. Simply because Mount Tai is the eastern sacred mountain (Dongyue) does not justify calling "Dongyue Dadi" as "Taishan Dadi." (2) The disputed trademark, through long-term promotion and use, has formed a stable market order and has not produced adverse effects. Cancelling the disputed trademark would be extremely unfair to Wanjia Company and detrimental to protecting the interests of consumers. "Dongyue Dadi" is a fixed appellation for a Taoist deity. Ordinary consumers, upon seeing the term "Taishan Dadi," will not associate it with "Dongyue Dadi" or generate religious associations, nor will it affect religious sentiments. Moreover, whether a trademark has adverse effects is closely related to the goods on which it is registered. The disputed trademark is registered for use on building materials such as gypsum, which will not cause desecration or derogation of "Taishan Dadi" or harm the religious sentiments of the relevant public. (3) Taishan Gypsum Company's initiation of this trademark dispute is, in essence, an act of using public interest as a pretext to harm competitors. Taishan Gypsum Company previously applied for a trademark dispute on the grounds that "Taishan and diagram" trademark constituted similar trademarks on identical or similar goods as the disputed trademark, which was not supported by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board. It then turned to the "adverse effects" ground to file the trademark dispute, indicating that its intention in filing the dispute was improper and also reflecting that it did not believe "Taishan Dadi" harmed religious sentiments and folk beliefs or caused adverse effects. (4) Taishan Gypsum Company's claim that "the disputed trademark was improperly registered" is unrelated to the facts and law of this case. Whether the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes squatting, whether the disputed trademark is similar to the "Taishan and diagram" trademark, and Wanjia Company's application for a series of trademarks are not within the scope of trial in this case. In summary, the second-instance judgment had clear findings of fact and correctly applied the law, and Wanjia Company requests this court to uphold it.

During this court's retrial review, Taishan Gypsum Company submitted the following evidence: 1. First group of evidence, including the "Explanation on Folk Religious Belief Activities in the Taishan Scenic Area" issued by the Tai'an City Taishan Scenic Area Management Committee, the explanation of Mount Tai on Baidu, the retrieval report from the National Library, the explanation of the Five Sacred Mountain Emperors (Wuyue Dadi) on Baidu, the explanation of Dongyue Taishan Tianqi Rensheng Dadi, and the explanation on the Dadi website, intended to prove that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a religious idol. 2. Second group of evidence, the defense statement for the opposition against the registration of Trademark No. 9044267 "Taishan Dadi," intended to prove that Wanjia Company also knew that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. 3. Third group of evidence, including relevant court judgments, labor dispute arbitration commission awards, decisions, and investigation reports, intended to prove that Wanjia Company engaged in improper registration acts. Subsequently, it additionally submitted twenty-eight pieces of evidence, including the "Explanation on the Belief in 'Taishan Dadi'" issued by the Tai'an Taoist Association, the "Explanation on the Folk Custom and Belief of 'Taishan Dadi'" issued by the Tai'an City People's Government, "Taishan Culture Writes a New Chapter" published by Shandong People's Publishing House, "Common Knowledge Questions and Answers on Taoism" published by Shanghai People's Publishing House, the China Taoist Association website, the Hebei Taoist Association website, the Longhu Mountain Taoist Association website, the Chinese Taoism Forum, the China Ethnic and Religious Network, the China Mazu Network, and other websites and newspapers introducing the Five Sacred Mountain Emperors, intended to prove that "Taishan Dadi" is a commonly used appellation for a Taoist deity.

Wanjia Company commented on the above evidence, stating that the explanatory note from the Tai'an City Taishan Scenic Area Management Committee and the retrieval report from the National Library have weak probative value. The Tai'an City Taishan Scenic Area Management Committee is not a religious administrative body, and its understanding of religious terms may inevitably deviate compared to religious figures and believers. Moreover, since both the committee and Taishan Gypsum Company are located in Tai'an City, the authenticity, legality, and relevance of this note are questionable. The National Library's retrieval report on "Taishan Dadi" includes a total of 34 newspaper and journal articles. Most of these articles are news reports on society, folk customs, and tourism, or even financial articles, without strong professionalism. The authors are mostly not religious figures or historical experts and do not have much understanding of the distinction between the appellations "Taishan Dadi" and "Dongyue Dadi," and may mistakenly believe that "Taishan Dadi" is an alias for "Dongyue Dadi." Furthermore, the retrieval time spans from 1991 to 2014, a period of 20 years, and only 34 articles contain "Taishan Dadi." Therefore, based on the retrieval reports, the group using the term "Taishan Dadi" is mostly not religious figures or believers, the number of uses is small, and the extent of coverage is not broad. Even if there are instances in reality where "Taishan Dadi" is used to refer to a Taoist deity, it only proves the behavior of a small number of people and is insufficient to prove that the appellation "Taishan Dadi" has been widely accepted by Taoist followers or has become an appellation for a Taoist deity. The explanatory note issued by the Tai'an Taoist Association constitutes witness testimony. The witness should appear in court; without their appearance, the probative value is weak. Moreover, the note merely states the situation of belief in "Taishan Dadi" and does not explain what adverse effects would arise from using "Taishan Dadi" as a trademark. The explanatory note issued by the Tai'an City People's Government repeatedly uses "Taishan Dadi" and "Dongyue Dadi" in parallel, but the specific descriptions still primarily use "Taishan Shen" and "Dongyue Dadi." Moreover, the names included in the national intangible cultural heritage list and the third batch of world intangible cultural heritage announced by the Shandong Provincial People's Government are "Dongyue Temple Fair" and "Dongyue Dadi," without using "Taishan Dadi." This sufficiently proves that even if the appellation "Taishan Dadi" exists, it is not the formal appellation for the deity. Although six of the pieces of evidence mention the appellation "Taishan Dadi," they only indicate that there are instances in reality where "Dongyue Taishan Dadi" or "Dongyue Dadi" is abbreviated as "Taishan Dadi," which is insufficient to prove that "Taishan Dadi" has been widely accepted by Taoist followers or has become an appellation for a Taoist deity. Twenty of the pieces of evidence use "Dongyue Taishan Dadi" and "Dongyue Dadi" without using "Taishan Dadi" alone. "Dongyue Taishan Dadi" is a fixed appellation for a deity and should not be abbreviated to "Taishan Dadi." It also cannot prove that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity, let alone that its use as a trademark application has adverse effects.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board agreed with Taishan Gypsum Company's opinion.

Wanjia Company submitted four pieces of evidence, including printouts of web pages from the China Taoist Association and local Taoist associations and Dongyue Temple websites, partial printouts of the Tai'an City Ethnic and Religious Affairs Bureau webpage, and two administrative judgments, intended to prove that "Taishan Dadi" is not an appellation for a Taoist deity and that matters involving only harm to specific civil rights and interests should not be deemed as falling within Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law.

Taishan Gypsum Company presented its opinions on the authenticity of the above evidence, arguing that Wanjia Company's evidence was one-sided, as "Taishan Dadi" also appears on the websites of Taoist associations, and "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. The "adverse effects" stipulated in Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law only require the possibility of causing adverse effects, not the actual occurrence of adverse effects.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board agreed with Taishan Gypsum Company's opinion.

This court holds that, based on the reasons for Taishan Gypsum Company's application for retrial, the defense opinions of Wanjia Company and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board, and the facts found, the focus of the dispute in this case is: Whether the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes a circumstance of "other adverse effects" as stipulated in Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law.

Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law stipulates that signs that are detrimental to socialist morality or customs or have other adverse effects shall not be used as trademarks. When determining whether a particular sign constitutes a situation with other adverse effects, consideration should be given to whether the sign or its constituent elements may produce negative or adverse effects on China's political, economic, cultural, religious, ethnic, and other social public interests and public order. If a sign has religious connotations, regardless of whether the relevant public can generally recognize it, or whether the sign has been used and has gained a certain level of recognition, it can generally be considered that the registration of the sign is detrimental to religious sentiments, religious beliefs, or folk beliefs, and has adverse effects. In this case, books submitted by Wanjia Company, such as the "Tai'an City Annals," "Tai'an Prefecture Annals," and "Dictionary of Chinese Deities and Monsters," as well as websites such as the China Taoist Association website, record that Dongyue Taishan Dadi is one of the Taoist deities, also known as "Dongyue Dadi," "Taishan Shen," "Dongyue Rensheng Tianqi Wang," and "Taishan Fujun." It is a mountain god in Taoism and the ruler of the underworld, who has not only been enshrined by successive emperors but also long worshipped by common people and Taoist followers, holding a very high religious status. In the introductions of "Dongyue Dadi" or "Taishan Shen," no mention is made of "Taishan Dadi." A smaller number of books submitted by Taishan Gypsum Company, such as "Taishan Culture Writes a New Chapter" and "Common Knowledge Questions and Answers on Taoism," as well as news reports and academic papers, mention that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity. This court holds that determining whether "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity and whether it has religious connotations requires consideration not only of the evidence submitted by the parties in this case but also of the recognition of relevant religious institutions and individuals, as well as the long historical origins and social reality of Taoism's widespread popularity among Chinese folk believers. First, although most of the evidence submitted by the parties, consistent with the official records identified by the court of second instance, does not record that "Dongyue Dadi" or "Taishan Shen" is called "Taishan Dadi," some books, news reports, and academic papers mention that "Dongyue Dadi" or "Taishan Shen" is called "Taishan Dadi." Second, the Tai'an City Ethnic and Religious Affairs Bureau and the Tai'an Taoist Association have also issued explanations proving that "Taishan Dadi" is an appellation for a Taoist deity, and their recognition itself reflects the understanding of relevant religious institutions and individuals. Third, Taoism is a religion with a long historical tradition in China. Over the long course of history, Taoism has had a broad base of believers, and there are numerous books, magazines, and reports documenting Taoism. Therefore, it is difficult to say that the appellations for Taoist deities are limited to official state records. Therefore, even if the official records recognized by the court of second instance did not record "Taishan Dadi" as "Taishan Shen" or "Dongyue Dadi," and "Taishan Dadi" is not the only corresponding appellation for "Dongyue Dadi" or "Taishan Shen," the relevant evidence and the recognition of religious institutions and individuals demonstrate that "Taishan Dadi" consistently refers to "Taishan Shen" or "Dongyue Dadi," and not to other Taoist deities. The appellation "Taishan Dadi" objectively exists and has religious connotations. Wanjia Company and the original applicant for the registration of the disputed trademark registered and used "Taishan Dadi" as a trademark, which may cause harm to religious beliefs, religious sentiments, or folk beliefs, thereby causing adverse effects. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark falls within the circumstances stipulated in Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law and should be revoked.

In summary, Ruling No. 051795 of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and the first-instance judgment are correct and should be upheld. The second-instance judgment had basically clear factual findings but erroneous application of the law and should be reversed. Pursuant to Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item (8) of the Trademark Law (as amended in 2001), Article 89, Paragraph 1, Item (2) and Paragraph 3 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 76, Paragraph 1 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. Reverse the Administrative Judgment (2014) Gao Xing (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 3390 of the Beijing High People's Court;
2. Uphold the Administrative Judgment (2014) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 6325 of the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court.

The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 and the second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100, totaling RMB 200, shall be borne by Shandong Wanjia Building Materials Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
